text:
Nobody can tell what you sell. That's the whole problem.

On Tech Thursday we pulled up a real business page, live, on screen. Good design. Nice colors. Ten seconds in, none of us could say what the event was, who was performing, or when it happened.

Meanwhile Pew found that more than a third of new web pages since ChatGPT show signs of AI writing. Volume is free now. Clarity isn't.

Run the 3-second test on your own page:

1. What is this? Name it plainly, not cleverly.
2. Who is it for? For everyone means for no one.
3. What's the proof? Reviews, years, receipts. Not adjectives.
4. What's the one action? Five calls to action is zero.
5. Then hand it to AI: make the offer clear and the experience emphasized, then give me a minimalist version for social.

That last prompt is the one we ran on the show. It pulled fifteen years of experience up to the top and cut everything that was competing with it.

text:
Do it the hard way once. Then never again.

The reason automations break is that nobody ran the job by hand first. You can't compress a process you've never actually done.

We build everything here the slow way to start. Manually, badly, all the way through. Then we go back and cut, and what survives is a workflow that holds, because by then we know which steps were load-bearing.

Automate what you understand. Not what you assume.
